title: Investigating the safety and efficacy of the early use of plerixafor in healthy stem cell donors
official: A Phase 2 Proof of Concept Clinical Trial to Determine the Safety and Efficacy of Pre-emptive Plerixafor to aid G-CSF Mobilised Peripheral Blood Stem Cell Collections in Healthy Donors (PREEMPT-HD)
summary:
Background and study aims
There is increasing demand for healthy unrelated stem cell donors for patients requiring a stem cell transplant. Only 17% of donations proceed on the first-choice date, leading to delays for patients. 10% of donations collect less than the target cell dose, worsening outcomes. At Anthony Nolan 27% of donations require two days. Evidence shows that outcomes for donors improve following a one-day collection, they experience less side effects and recover more quickly.

Plerixafor is a medication given in addition to the current injections used to prepare donors. It increases the number of stem cells collected by encouraging stem cells from the bone marrow into the bloodstream. It has been used effectively and safely for many years in people who are donating stem cells for their own future treatment.

Plerixafor is currently used 'off-label' in healthy donors however medical evidence shows it is safe in this setting. UK and World Marrow Donor Association (WMDA) consensus statements were published recently supporting its use in healthy donors.

This trial will utilise plerixafor upfront in donors predicted to require a two-day donation. The aim is to increase the number of stem cells collected, improving outcomes for patients and to collect the cells in one day, improving donor experience.

Who can participate?
Consenting donors who are predicted to require a two-day collection (using our predictive model) will be eligible. 

What does the study involve?
Donors will attend before their donation for an additional blood test to see how many stem cells are in their blood. Donors who have low numbers will receive plerixafor.

All donors who receive plerixafor and a matched control group will have 1-2mls of the donation frozen for a further project to understand the difference in the product after plerixafor. Donors will complete additional donor experience questionnaires. 40 donors will receive plerixafor on trial over a period of 2 years.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Benefits: A donor who takes part in this study may receive plerixafor, which could enable stem cell collection to be completed in a single day, reducing the likelihood of needing a second donation visit. A one-day donation may reduce side effects and complications associated with the donation procedure and allow the donor to return home sooner. Even if a donor does not receive plerixafor, participation may provide greater confidence that the donation process can be completed in one day. In addition, all donors who participate will contribute to research aimed at improving the donation process for future donors and helping ensure timely access to stem cell transplants for patients.
Risks: All donors who agree to be enrolled in the study will require an extra 4 ml blood test on the evening before or the morning of the donation. Blood tests are generally safe, but potential complications can include bruising, fainting, pain, or infection at the site. This test is an important step in the trial design as it will ensure that we only administer   plerixafor to donors who will benefit from the injection. This has been discussed with the donor panel and focus group, and the time required for this and the additional visit to the hospital was not felt to be an excessive additional burden. Donors reported that given they will be in the local area already, in preparation for their donation, this would not be a significant concern. Donors also felt that confirmation of a one day donation was an overall benefit.
All donors on the study will receive G CSF injections as standard for four days prior to the donation. After these injections, if the blood test suggests low circulating numbers of stem cells in the blood, they will be offered plerixafor on the trial. This will be administered as an injection, under the skin in a similar way to the G CSF injections; however, a nurse will administer the medication at the collection centre. Plerixafor is considered safe in healthy donors, however there are side effects related to this medication. The main concerns are nausea and diarrhoea, as well as redness at the site of the injection. These side effects are a concern for donors, especially if they occur during the procedure, as highlighted by the donor panel. This feedback altered the design of the trial, to deliver the plerixafor the night before, if possible, to reduce the risk of side effects occurring while on the machine. The participant information leaflet clearly defines the chances of these side effects and any rare but serious complications. It is an important outcome of the trial to report the incidence and severity of these side effects and the impact on donor experience, which will be captured in the follow up questionnaires. The expectation is that these will not outweigh the benefits of a one day collection, which reduces side effects of the actual procedure and enables donors to go home sooner. However, the trial is designed to answer this specific question, and this is clearly explained to donors in the participant information leaflet.
With any clinical trial, especially one bridging multiple organisations (Nottingham University Hospital, Anthony Nolan and the Royal Marsden NHS Foundation Trust), there is a burden of data collection and a risk of a breach of confidentiality. Data collection in MACRO will be anonymised, and the Anthony Nolan data manager has been involved in the development of all protocols. Data will be subject to the data management policies at all organisations, and information about data management will be included in the donor participant information leaflet and consent form.
The sponsor has a risk assessment and mitigations in place, which will be monitored by the trial management group.
In relation to the burden for participants, the appointment during which participants will provide informed consent involves significant amounts of information and consent forms for the standard of care procedure. This creates an additional burden, and there is a concern that this may be too much for donors to absorb. To mitigate this burden, both standard of care and trial information will be sent to donors in advance of the appointment, including the participant information leaflet and consent forms. This has been discussed with the donor focus group, who feel that donors expect this information and that, if provided in an accessible format, it will not be problematic. The additional time required is acknowledged; however, donors are already expecting a long day and this is not anticipated to have a significant additional impact. The donor information leaflet and consent form have been reviewed by the donor panel, Research Review Board and patient services team, with changes made in response to feedback to ensure information is comprehensive but accessible.
All donors enrolled on the trial will be asked to complete additional follow up questionnaires on top of the standard follow up carried out by the Anthony Nolan follow up team. These will be much shorter and should take only a few minutes to complete. They are essential for accurate reporting of donor outcomes and experiences. This has been discussed with the donor panel and focus group, who feel that donors engaging with the trial will also be engaged with follow up and that this additional burden would not be concerning. The questionnaires will minimise repetition, and the number of donors asked to complete them will be limited to reduce overall burden.

Where is the study run from?
Royal Marsden NHS Foundation Trust (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
November 2026 to May 2029

Who is funding the study?
Anthony Nolan (UK)

conditions: Healthy volunteer donors for stem cell transplantation
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Participants must have a minimum age of 16 and maximum of 65 years
2. Participants must be healthy donors for allogeneic stem cell transplantation who are eligible to donate via the peripheral blood stem cell method in line with the Anthony Nolan suitability guidelines) and Joint UK Blood Transfusion and Tissue Transplantation Services Professional Advisory Committee (JPAC) guidelines (Bone Marrow and Peripheral Blood Stem Cell) as per AN Doc1796 (Collection centre procedures)  
3. Participants must have an Anthony Nolan predictive score of < 3 (range 0–6) following the medical assessment, indicating a higher likelihood of requiring two collection days for successful hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) harvest. 
4. People of childbearing potential must have a negative pregnancy test within 7 days prior to plerixafor administration. 
5. People of childbearing potential agree to use highly effective contraceptive measure as follows: 
a) combined (oestrogen and progestogen containing) hormonal contraception associated with inhibition of ovulation: 
   - oral 
   - intravaginal  
   - transdermal  
 b) progestogen-only hormonal contraception associated with inhibition of ovulation: 
   - oral  
   - injectable  
   - implantable 
 c) intrauterine device (IUD) 
 d) intrauterine hormone-releasing system (IUS) 
 e) bilateral tubal occlusion 
 f) vasectomised partner 
 g) sexual abstinence 
6. Willing and able to provide written informed consent. 
7. Neutrophil count < 50x10*9/L and normal platelet count prior to administration
Exclusion criteria:
1. The recipient’s transplant centre have opted out of receiving plerixafor stimulated products on the verification form 
2. History of CTCAE Grade 2 diarrhoea or vomiting associated with G-CSF injections. 
3. People of childbearing potential who are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding
4. Known allergy to plerixafor or excipient ingredients
